title: Pesticides and personal, public and environmental safety

lessons.title: Understanding pesticides and how they cause harm
lessons.html:
What pesticides are

A pesticide is any substance used to kill, repel or control a pest. In South African law most of these are called agricultural remedies. They are grouped by target: insecticides (insects), rodenticides (rats and mice), herbicides (weeds), fungicides (fungi), acaricides (mites and ticks) and fumigants (gases that penetrate stored products and structures).

Formulations

The same active ingredient can be sold in different formulations, each with different risks:

  • Emulsifiable concentrates and suspension concentrates are diluted with water and sprayed. The concentrate is the most hazardous stage.
  • Wettable powders and dusts can be inhaled during mixing.
  • Granules and baits are less hazardous to the applicator but attractive to children, pets and wildlife.
  • Gels used for cockroaches are placed precisely and are low-risk when applied correctly.
  • Fumigants such as phosphine-generating tablets release highly toxic gas.

Routes of exposure

RouteHow it happens
Skin (dermal)Splashes, contaminated gloves or clothing; the most common route
InhalationSpray mist, dust, vapour and fumigant gas
Swallowing (oral)Eating or smoking with contaminated hands, decanted chemicals in drink bottles
EyesSplashes during mixing

Toxicity and hazard

Toxicity is how poisonous a substance is. Hazard depends on toxicity and exposure together. A highly toxic product used in a closed bait station may present low hazard, while a moderately toxic spray used carelessly indoors can be very hazardous. Labels in South Africa carry hazard information and colour-coded toxicity classification; always read them, and read the safety data sheet (SDS) for more detail.

Effects may be acute, appearing soon after exposure, or chronic, developing over months or years of repeated exposure.

lessons.title: Protecting yourself and your team
lessons.html:
Hierarchy of control

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 and its hazardous chemical regulations, employers must assess and control exposure. Apply controls in this order:

  1. Eliminate: is chemical treatment needed at all? Could sanitation or proofing solve the problem?
  2. Substitute with a less hazardous product or formulation, such as gel instead of spray.
  3. Engineering controls: closed mixing systems, bait stations, ventilation.
  4. Administrative controls: procedures, training, restricted entry, work rotation, medical surveillance where required.
  5. Personal protective equipment as the last line of defence.

PPE

  • Chemical-resistant gloves (such as nitrile), not cotton or leather.
  • Overalls; a chemical apron when handling concentrates.
  • Goggles or a face shield during mixing.
  • Respirator with the correct cartridge when the label or SDS requires it. For fumigants, a full-face respirator with the correct canister or self-contained breathing apparatus as specified, with fit testing.
  • Chemical-resistant boots.

Inspect PPE before each use. Wash gloves before removing them. Wash work clothes separately from family laundry.

Safe work habits

  • Never eat, drink or smoke while working with pesticides.
  • Never decant pesticide into food or drink containers.
  • Mix only the amount needed.
  • Wash hands and face before breaks and shower at the end of the day.

Recognising poisoning

Signs vary by product but may include headache, dizziness, nausea, sweating, blurred vision, breathing difficulty, muscle twitching or collapse. If poisoning is suspected: remove the person from exposure without exposing yourself, remove contaminated clothing, rinse skin and eyes with plenty of clean water, and get medical help immediately. Take the label or SDS to the doctor. Follow the first aid instructions on the label and SDS. Hands-on first aid training by an accredited provider is required for anyone in this work.

lessons.title: Protecting the public and the environment
lessons.html:
Public safety

Pest management officers work in homes, schools, hospitals, restaurants, food factories and farms where untrained people are present. Their safety is your responsibility.

  • Inform occupants before treatment: what will be used, precautions and when it is safe to return.
  • Remove or cover food, utensils, toys, pet bowls and fish tanks.
  • Keep people and pets out of treated areas for the period stated on the label.
  • Use tamper-resistant, secured bait stations for rodenticides wherever children, pets or non-target animals may be present.
  • Never leave products, mixed spray or containers unattended.
  • Post warning notices where required, especially for fumigation.

Vulnerable people

Pregnant women, infants, the elderly and people with asthma or other illnesses may be more sensitive. Ask about them during planning and adjust the method or timing.

Environmental protection

  • Water: do not spray near rivers, dams, boreholes or drains unless the product is registered for that situation. Never rinse equipment into water.
  • Bees and pollinators: avoid spraying flowering plants and follow label bee warnings.
  • Wildlife and pets: secondary poisoning occurs when owls, raptors, dogs or cats eat poisoned rodents. Search for and remove carcasses, and use rodenticides strictly as labelled.
  • Drift: do not spray in wind conditions the label warns against.

Transport, storage and disposal

Transport pesticides in a secured, ventilated compartment separate from the driver, food and passengers, in original labelled containers, with a spill kit. Store in a locked, ventilated store. Triple rinse empty containers where the label allows, render them unusable and dispose of them through an approved route in line with the Waste Act 59 of 2008. Never burn or bury them.

Key points

  • Skin contact is the most common route of exposure; inhalation is the most dangerous for fumigants.
  • Apply the hierarchy of control, with PPE as the last line of defence.
  • Recognise poisoning signs and act immediately: remove from exposure, decontaminate, get medical help with the label.
  • Protect occupants, children and pets with notices, re-entry times and secured bait stations.
  • Prevent contamination of water, pollinators and wildlife, and dispose of containers correctly.
